title: Reinforcing What the Student Has Learned: Teacher-Guided On-Policy Distillation

paper.title: Reinforcing What the Student Has Learned: Teacher-Guided On-Policy Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model reasoning through dense teacher feedback on student-generated responses.
We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher–student log-probability difference of mathematical positions.
Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher’s expression.
We instead take the student’s own pretrained base as a reference: the student–base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student’s distance from the teacher.
Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation ( SD-OPD ), which uses centered student–base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher–student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round.
Across 5 teacher–student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/aim-uofa/sd-opd .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach in which a language model learns from a teacher on responses generated by its own current policy ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2023 ) . The teacher scores every token at prefixes the student visits, so supervision is dense and lies on the student’s own trajectories. As the student changes, new responses are sampled and scored, and the training distribution follows the student’s current behavior, as in imitation learning on learner-induced states ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . This combination of on-policy sampling and token-level feedback has supported both capability transfer from larger teachers to smaller students ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) and the consolidation of specialized teachers into a single model ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) . However, the effectiveness of OPD depends on how teacher feedback is constructed and weighted ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In sampled-token OPD, the magnitude of teacher–student log-probability differences determines the strength of token-level supervision ( Gu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Post-training also shifts a model’s preferences for wording and formatting ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) , so teacher–student disagreement reflects differences in expression as well as gaps in reasoning. Weighting updates by this disagreement thus spends update strength on the teacher’s expression as well as its reasoning. This raises two questions: how is update strength distributed across tokens, and can it come from a source other than teacher disagreement? For the first question, on DAPO-Math responses, style-related positions have 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher–student log-probability difference of mathematical positions (Figure 2 ). For the second, we compare the student with its own pretrained base ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , which records the token preferences the student has already acquired, independently of its distance from the teacher. These preferences include reasoning expressions such as suppose , try , and strategy , but their amplitude is also concentrated at style-related positions, with a style-to-mathematics ratio of 4.1, so they need selection. We select them by teacher sign agreement, keeping a student preference only where the teacher favors the same direction. This test retains very different shares of preferences with similar strength (Figure 3 ) and lowers the style-to-mathematics ratio to 3.1, whereas the same test with teacher–student magnitudes still leaves 3.7 (Section 3.2 ). These findings lead to Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation ( SD-OPD ; Figure 1 ). Centered student–base log-probability differences supply the coefficients, and a coefficient is kept only when its sign agrees with centered teacher–student feedback. The teacher thus decides which student preferences to develop, but its disagreement magnitude does not scale the updates. The teacher and base stay frozen, while the student signal is recomputed after each training round, so it covers both the initial post-training changes and those acquired during distillation. We evaluate SD-OPD in 5 teacher–student configurations with three teachers and Qwen3 students of 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters, using six mathematics benchmarks and matched rollout and response budgets. SD-OPD outperforms OPD on every benchmark in every configuration and achieves the highest six-task student average in all 5 configurations (Table 1 ). Average gains range from 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points over OPD and from 3.45 to 14.89 over ExOPD. Our contributions are as follows: • A diagnosis of how OPD weights its updates. We show that teacher–student disagreement is not a neutral measure of what the student should learn: its mean absolute magnitude is 3.5 times larger at style-related than at mathematical positions, the gap persists with a larger teacher and on GSM8K, and sign-agreement filtering does not remove it while teacher–student differences set the magnitude. • The student’s own post-training changes as a source of supervision. We show that the difference between a post-trained student and its pretrained base can set update strength, with the teacher deciding only which directions to reinforce. SD-OPD implements this division of roles and recomputes the student signal every round, so update strength follows what the current student prefers rather than how far it is from the teacher. It improves over OPD in every evaluated configuration and lets an 8B student exceed the average accuracy of its Qwen3-30B-A3B teacher. sections.heading: On-policy knowledge distillation.
sections.text: Knowledge distillation transfers teacher predictions to a student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , while sequence-level distillation trains on teacher-generated targets ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . Teacher-generated reasoning data extend this approach to mathematical and code reasoning ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Guha et al., 2026 ) . GKD and MiniLLM obtain supervision on student-generated sequences through distribution matching and reverse-KL policy optimization ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2023 ) . DistiLLM combines skew-divergence objectives with reuse of student outputs, while DistiLLM-2 contrasts teacher- and student-generated responses ( Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) . Black-box OPD learns feedback from a discriminator trained on teacher and student text ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . Recent work also studies local distribution matching and token-specific supervision weights ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In these methods, teacher outputs determine the strength of supervision; SD-OPD instead takes update strength from the student’s own post-training changes and uses the teacher only to select their direction.

sections.heading: Self-distillation and contextual supervision.
sections.text: Context-conditioned self-teaching obtains additional information from reference solutions in Self-Distilled Reasoner ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , textual feedback in SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , and demonstrations in SDFT ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . On-Policy Context Distillation also learns from a context-conditioned teacher, including configurations with different teacher and student sizes ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . In these approaches, the additional supervision comes from privileged information placed in the teacher’s context; in SD-OPD , it comes from the student’s own post-training history, measured against a fixed base model, with an independent teacher constraining its direction.

sections.heading: Post-training differences and delta distillation.
sections.text: URIAL analyzes changes between aligned and base token distributions, including changes in expression ( Lin et al., 2024 ) ; we turn this comparison into a training signal. Policy–reference log-ratios connect preference optimization to implicit rewards ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) ; implicit process reward models and PRIME extend this connection to dense reasoning feedback learned from outcome labels ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . G-OPD introduces a reference policy and reward scaling; its ExOPD variant studies extrapolation with both an initial-student reference and a teacher pre-RL reference ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . OPD 2 also uses centering and a same-sign condition, but its primary signal is a teacher–base difference ( Heo et al., 2026 ) . SD-OPD instead uses the current student’s changes relative to the student’s own base, recomputed every round, and lets teacher feedback decide which directions to reinforce. sections.heading: 3 Observations
sections.text: We compare teacher–student disagreement with the student’s own post-training changes, using the initial student S 0 S_{0} (Qwen3-1.7B), its pretrained base S B S_{B} (Qwen3-1.7B-Base), and teacher T T (Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507). All analyses use all eight responses to each of the same 1,024 questions sampled without replacement from DAPO-Math-17K ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . This gives 8,192 responses with about 11.3 million response tokens. All three models then score the same token IDs at the same causal prefixes, using full-vocabulary log-softmax normalization. Appendix C gives generation and scoring details, and Appendix D repeats the category-level analyses with another teacher and on GSM8K.

sections.heading: 3.1 Teacher–Student Disagreement Varies across Token Categories
sections.text: To compare teacher–student disagreement across token categories, we use the sampled-token log-ratio feedback studied in OPD ( Gu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . For response token y t y_{t} at prefix h t = ( x , y < t ) h_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) , this feedback is r t = log ⁡ p T ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) − log ⁡ p S 0 ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) . r_{t}=\log p_{T}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})-\log p_{S_{0}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t}). (1) We categorize token positions using fixed textual rules. Style-related positions include discourse wording, answer labels, and Markdown formatting, while mathematical positions include numbers, operators, formula variables, a fixed mathematical lexicon, and logical expressions. Markup, whitespace, and other tokens form separate groups; Appendix C details the classification. Because the categories differ in frequency (about 0.6 million style-related and 4.7 million mathematical tokens, both present in every response), we compare per-token means rather than totals. For positions 𝒯 i , j , c \mathcal{T}_{i,j,c} in category c c of response j j to question i i , we compute the per-token mean M i , j , c ​ ( r ) = 1 | 𝒯 i , j , c | ​ ∑ t ∈ 𝒯 i , j , c | r i , j , t | . M_{i,j,c}(r)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i,j,c}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i,j,c}}|r_{i,j,t}|. (2) We average these values equally over the eight responses to each question and then equally over questions, preventing longer responses from receiving extra weight.

sections.heading: Style-related positions have larger feedback amplitudes.
sections.text: Figure 2 (a) shows mean absolute feedback of 1.226 at style-related positions and 0.347 at mathematical positions, a 3.5-fold difference. OPD uses this log-ratio as a coefficient in token-level policy gradients ( Gu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , so for the initial student, style-related positions receive larger coefficients on average. For example, differences in wording or formatting receive large coefficients even when the student expresses the same mathematical idea.

sections.heading: 3.2 Student Preferences and Teacher Selection
sections.text: Since teacher disagreement mixes expression with reasoning, we look for a reference that measures update strength from what the student has already learned. The student’s own pretrained base provides one: comparing student and base predictions at shared prefixes reveals preferences acquired during post-training, including how the student expresses mathematical reasoning ( Lin et al., 2024 ) . On the same responses and prefixes, we define d t = log ⁡ p S 0 ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) − log ⁡ p S B ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) . d_{t}=\log p_{S_{0}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})-\log p_{S_{B}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t}). (3) The sign of d t d_{t} indicates whether the observed token has become more probable ( d t > 0 d_{t}>0 ) or less probable ( d t < 0 d_{t}<0 ) relative to the base at that prefix. Since the reference is the pretrained base, this difference summarizes cumulative changes across post-training.

sections.heading: Acquired preferences favor exploration and planning.
sections.text: Figure 3 (a–b) shows the strings whose probability post-training raised or lowered most. The raised strings are reasoning moves rather than formatting: they form hypotheses and explore alternatives ( suppose , maybe , try ), plan and organize a solution ( strategy , idea , structure ), and test candidates ( plug , examine ). The lowered strings instead narrate routine computation ( calculations , distribute , rewrite ) or assert that a step is easy or correct ( straightforward , ensuring ), and their shifts are much smaller. Post-training has thus mainly added ways of deciding how to approach a problem, rather than removing old habits of describing computations. These changes reflect how this particular student learned to reason, and a teacher trained differently need not share them. The student–base difference therefore records reasoning behavior the student has already acquired, which makes it a natural source of supervision for further distillation. Not every shift is desirable, however: the checking step verify is also lowered, so these changes still need selection.

sections.heading: Teacher agreement selects which acquired preferences to reinforce.
sections.text: These changes also include stylistic preferences, with a style-to-mathematics ratio of 4.1 (Figure 2 (b)). We therefore keep d t d_{t} only where the teacher agrees in sign, using the mask m t = 𝟏 [ r t d t > 0 ] m_{t}=\mathbf{1}[r_{t}d_{t}>0] . This test separates preferences of similar strength (Figure 3 (c)): try and strategy keep only 19.3% and 13.8% of their absolute amplitude, whereas idea keeps 71.4%. For straightforward , it keeps the decrease and removes occurrences where the student raised its probability. Across categories, it removes 69.1% of the style-related but 58.7% of the mathematical amplitude, lowering the ratio to 3.1 (Figure 2 (d)).

sections.heading: The magnitude source sets the gated balance.
sections.text: The mask m t m_{t} decides which positions and directions are retained, while the magnitude source decides their relative weight. To isolate the magnitude source, we apply the same mask to teacher–student feedback and compare m t ​ r t m_{t}r_{t} with m t ​ d t m_{t}d_{t} (Figure 2 (c–d)). Gated teacher–student coefficients are smaller than raw feedback in every category, yet style-related positions still receive 0.380 versus 0.102 at mathematical positions, a ratio of 3.7 compared with 3.5 before filtering. Student–base magnitudes lower the style-related amplitude by 40.3% and the mathematical amplitude from 0.102 to 0.074, giving a ratio of 3.1 instead. Because both signals retain identical positions and a uniform rescaling of OPD would leave the ratio unchanged, this difference comes from the magnitude source rather than from filtering. These patterns also hold with another teacher and on GSM8K (Appendix D ). These observations motivate combining student-derived strength with teacher-guided selection. sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: All trained models use DAPO-Math-17K prompts ( Yu et al., 2026 ) for 272 rollout rounds, corresponding to one full pass over the training dataset (one epoch). Each round samples 64 prompts and four responses per prompt. The learning rate is 10 − 6 10^{-6} and the response batch size is 64. We match rollout and response budgets across methods and evaluate their final checkpoints. Appendices A.1 and A.3 detail the shared training hyperparameters and method-specific clipping settings, respectively.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: We evaluate on six mathematics benchmarks: AIME24 and AIME25 ( zhuzilin, 2025a ; zhuzilin, 2025b ) , AIME26 and HMMT25 (February) from MathArena ( Dekoninck et al., 2026 ) , AMC23 ( math-ai, 2025 ) , and MATH500 ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ; Lightman et al., 2024 ) . We sample 16 responses per problem in non-thinking mode and report pass@1 averaged over these samples (avg@16) on each benchmark. The evaluation protocol uses temperature 0.7, top- p p 0.8, top- k k 20, and a maximum response length of 38,912 tokens. We retain completed and truncated responses and check extracted final answers for normalized or symbolic equivalence.

sections.heading: Gains over OPD on every benchmark and setting.
sections.text: Table 1 shows that SD-OPD improves six-task average pass@1 over OPD by 7.76–10.37 percentage points across all 5 teacher–student configurations. The improvements hold on every benchmark in every configuration, covering all 30 comparisons under matched rollout and response budgets, and SD-OPD achieves the highest six-task student average in every configuration.

sections.heading: Gains across teachers.
sections.text: The gains do not depend on a particular teacher family. For Qwen3-1.7B, average gains over OPD are 9.77, 9.99, and 8.64 percentage points for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, and MiMo-7B-RL-0530 teachers, respectively. ExOPD improves the average with both Qwen3 teachers, but falls below OPD with MiMo: 44.40% versus 50.65%, a 6.25-point decrease. In the same MiMo setting, SD-OPD reaches 59.29%, exceeding ExOPD by 14.89 points under the shared-vocabulary protocol in Appendix A.4 .

sections.heading: Gains across student sizes.
sections.text: Using Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 as the teacher, average gains over OPD are 9.99, 7.76, and 10.37 percentage points for the 1.7B, 4B, and 8B students, respectively. The margin over ExOPD is smallest for the 4B student (3.45 points) and widens to 9.07 points for the 8B student. Across all 5 configurations, SD-OPD also exceeds ExOPD on 28 of the 30 benchmark comparisons.

sections.heading: Students can surpass their teachers.
sections.text: Distilled from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, the 8B student reaches 76.11% average pass@1, exceeding the teacher’s 73.82% by 2.29 points, while OPD and ExOPD remain below it; this student also exceeds the teacher on AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25, and AMC23. On individual benchmarks, the 4B student also exceeds this teacher on AIME25 and AMC23, and the 1.7B student exceeds MiMo on AMC23 and MATH500.

sections.heading: 5.3 Ablation Study
sections.text: The two ablations test the two design choices of Section 4 in the 4B-to-1.7B setting: Ungated asks whether student-derived strength needs teacher selection, and Frozen asks whether the student signal must be refreshed.

sections.heading: Teacher guidance.
sections.text: Ungated uses A S A_{S} directly, with the same candidate approximation, replacing g ​ A S gA_{S} and removing teacher scoring. Its pass@1 is zero on all six tasks (Table 2 ). All 10,560 responses complete within 5–13 tokens, including the termination token, with a mean of 6.05 tokens. Appendix B.2 traces how these short, low-entropy responses emerge and explains them with a local gradient analysis: without the gate, the student–base signal reinforces deviations from the base.

sections.heading: 5.4 Training Dynamics
sections.text: To see how the choice of coefficient shapes the policy during training, Figure 4 tracks response length and policy entropy for OPD, ExOPD, and SD-OPD in the 30B-to-1.7B setting. We focus on the first 50 rollout steps, where the main differences emerge. Figure 4: Early training dynamics with Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 teaching Qwen3-1.7B. Each step is one rollout round with four optimizer updates. Length is the rollout mean; entropy averages the four logged update means. Curves are unsmoothed. Appendix B.1 shows all 272 training steps.

sections.heading: All three methods rapidly lengthen responses.
sections.text: Mean response length rises from approximately 1.7k tokens to around 6k within the first 20 steps. Over steps 41–50, OPD, ExOPD, and SD-OPD average 5.76k, 6.28k, and 6.45k tokens, respectively. ExOPD and SD-OPD reach similar lengths in this phase, although they build their coefficients differently.

sections.heading: SD-OPD develops a more concentrated policy.
sections.text: The entropy curves distinguish the methods more clearly. After an initial rise, SD-OPD entropy declines to an average of 0.158 nats over steps 41–50, compared with 0.314 for OPD and 0.308 for ExOPD. SD-OPD therefore keeps responses long while concentrating next-token predictions at the prefixes it visits. This pattern is consistent with reinforcing selected student preferences. Beyond step 50, the separation persists, with further gradual entropy reduction in SD-OPD and continuing length fluctuations (Appendix B.1 ).

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We showed that a student’s existing post-training changes can drive continued on-policy distillation. Since teacher–student disagreement is several times larger at style-related than at mathematical positions, SD-OPD instead takes update strength from student–base differences, constrains their direction with teacher feedback, and refreshes the student source throughout training. Across 5 teacher–student configurations, SD-OPD improves all six mathematics benchmarks over OPD and achieves higher six-task averages than both OPD and ExOPD. Average gains over OPD range from 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points when either the teacher or the student size changes. The ablations show that both components are needed: reinforcing student preferences without teacher feedback collapses all six benchmarks to zero, and fixing the student source falls below OPD. Further work can examine which of the student’s own post-training changes provide useful supervision, how their value evolves during training, and how they can support continued learning across tasks.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Our evaluation covers three teacher checkpoints from two families (Qwen3 and MiMo) and Qwen3 students of 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters on mathematical reasoning; extending SD-OPD to larger students and other domains is a natural next step. The comparisons match rollout and response budgets (clipping settings in Appendix A.3 ), and the token analysis uses fixed rule-based categories that apply unchanged across models and datasets. SD-OPD uses the student’s pretrained base, released with open model families such as Qwen3, and adds one base scoring pass per round. Top- K K centering ( K = 1,024 K=1{,}024 ) evaluates the centering sums over a shared candidate set at each prefix, using full-vocabulary probabilities.

sections.heading: A.4 Compatibility with the MiMo Teacher
sections.text: When distilling MiMo-7B-RL-0530 into Qwen3-1.7B, we align the response vocabulary and the prompt text while keeping each model’s own prompt tokenization.

sections.heading: Shared response vocabulary.
sections.text: The MiMo and Qwen3 output heads have 151,680 and 151,936 rows, respectively. Token IDs 0–151,664 are identical in the two tokenizers: they cover the 151,643 BPE tokens and the 22 special tokens from <|endoftext|> to <|file_sep|> , with the same normalization, pre-tokenization, and decoding. The vocabularies differ only beyond this range. Qwen3 adds four special tokens that MiMo lacks, <tool_response> , </tool_response> , <think> , and </think> (IDs 151,665–151,668), and the remaining rows of both heads (MiMo IDs 151,665–151,679 and Qwen3 IDs 151,669–151,935) are padding with no assigned token. We therefore restrict responses to the 151,665 shared IDs: a custom SGLang logit processor sets all other logits to − ∞ -\infty before sampling, and the old and updated student probabilities, policy entropy, and teacher and base scores are all normalized over this shared vocabulary. Excluding <think> and </think> from responses matches the non-thinking template, in which these tags appear only in the prompt. Model weights and output heads keep their original dimensions.

sections.heading: Prompt alignment.
sections.text: The common ChatML text appends /no_think to the user message and retains Qwen3’s empty thinking block in the assistant prefix. The student and base receive the original Qwen3 prompt IDs, including the prompt-only thinking tags. For MiMo, we decode the entire prompt while preserving special tokens and whitespace, then re-encode it with the teacher tokenizer. We append the sampled response IDs unchanged and align causal scores using the teacher’s re-encoded prompt length. This preserves the prompt text and response targets even when the two tokenizers produce different prompt lengths. After conversion, we check that the prompt and response fit within the teacher’s context length.

sections.heading: Scoring and optimization.
sections.text: We run the frozen MiMo teacher with its own Transformers model code and score the student responses by teacher forcing. OPD uses the sampled teacher–student log-ratio without centering or a base model. ExOPD uses the same teacher scorer, an extrapolation scale of λ = 1.25 \lambda=1.25 , and the frozen initial Qwen3-1.7B student as its reference, with all probabilities normalized over the shared vocabulary. For SD-OPD , the current student’s top K = 1,024 K=1{,}024 candidates include the sampled token, and centering uses probabilities normalized over the entire shared vocabulary, with no renormalization within the candidate set. The student–base coefficient and teacher gate otherwise follow Section 4 . In the MiMo setting, OPD, ExOPD, and SD-OPD share the vocabulary mask and prompt protocol, and all three use c dual = 3.0 c_{\mathrm{dual}}=3.0 .

sections.heading: Shared protocol and aggregation.
sections.text: All runs use seed 11, DAPO-Math-17K prompts, 64 prompts and four sampled responses per rollout step, and four optimizer updates per step. The learning rate, sampling settings, and response budget are shared; method-specific clipping follows Appendix A.3 . Response length averages all 256 generated responses, including those reaching the 7,168-token cap. sections.heading: The early separation persists later in training.
sections.text: The first 50 steps capture the rapid initial increase in response length and the emergence of a lower-entropy SD-OPD policy. Later length trajectories continue to fluctuate, while the entropy difference remains clear. Over the final 20 steps (253–272), mean lengths are 4.73k, 5.25k, and 6.52k tokens for OPD, ExOPD, and SD-OPD , respectively; the corresponding entropies are 0.323, 0.322, and 0.128 nats. For SD-OPD , the decrease from 0.158 nats over steps 41–50 to 0.128 over the final 20 steps is gradual relative to its initial decline. The longer-response, lower-entropy profile of SD-OPD thus persists beyond the main-text window, although none of the curves has fully plateaued. These statistics characterize each policy on the prefixes it generates. Lower token entropy indicates more concentrated next-token predictions at those prefixes. Under SD-OPD , responses stay long while these predictions become increasingly concentrated.

sections.heading: Observed training dynamics.
sections.text: In the 4B-to-1.7B ablation setting, the ungated run gradually collapses into short, low-entropy responses. Table B1 compares the training trajectories of Ungated and SD-OPD . For Ungated , mean response length first falls below 20 tokens at round 105 and reaches six tokens by round 180. The logged entropy initially rises, reaching 2.1405 at round 60, before falling to 0.0074 at round 120 and 0.0004 at round 272. The run thus passes through an early phase of growing uncertainty before collapsing onto a few tokens. SD-OPD retains a final training-rollout mean length of 6,176.3 tokens and logged entropy of 0.1243 under the same rollout budget and clipping configuration. The final evaluation confirms this collapse: none of the 10,560 Ungated responses is correct, and all are complete responses of only 5–13 tokens. Of these, 10,249 contain exactly six tokens.

sections.heading: The role of teacher guidance.
sections.text: The teacher gate supplies a direction test that is absent from Ungated : it blocks student coefficients whose signs disagree with centered teacher feedback. Both methods use the same dual-clipping constant, while task reward, entropy regularization, and auxiliary reference-KL penalties are disabled. Clipping controls the surrogate incentive for local probability-ratio changes, while the teacher gate selects which student-derived directions receive reinforcement. Together, the local analysis and the observed trajectories point to a self-reinforcing mechanism: without the gate, deviations amplified in one round become supervision in the next, and unguided preferences grow into degenerate behavior. The teacher’s direction test breaks this loop by admitting only the student changes the teacher also supports. Table B1: Training dynamics at selected rounds. sections.heading: C.1 Observation Protocol
sections.text: We sample 1,024 training questions and analyze all eight student responses per question, without filtering by correctness or length. Generation uses the non-thinking template, temperature 1.0, top- p p 1.0, no top- k k truncation, and at most 7,168 response tokens. The maximum context length is 8,275 tokens, and the per-question generation seed is 11 + 8 × dataset index 11+8\times\text{dataset index} . We use vLLM for generation ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) and Transformers for offline scoring ( Wolf et al., 2020 ) . The teacher, student, and base score identical token IDs at the same causal prefixes using untempered logits and full-vocabulary log-softmax. Log probabilities are computed in FP32 and differenced in FP64; all log probabilities and entropies use natural logarithms.

sections.heading: C.2 Token Categories
sections.text: We assign the five categories in Figure 2 using fixed English and Chinese phrase lists and textual rules, independently of model scores.

sections.heading: Style-related tokens.
sections.text: This category covers discourse wording, answer labels, and Markdown formatting used to organize or present a response. Examples include let’s , next , and finally ; line-initial Answer or Solution labels; and Markdown markers such as # and ** .

sections.heading: Mathematical tokens.
sections.text: This category covers numbers, operators, formula variables, mathematical vocabulary, and logical expressions used in derivations. Examples include numerals such as 3 3 and 12 12 , operators such as + + and = = , formula variables such as x x , and commands such as \frac and \sqrt . It also includes terms such as integer and triangle , and logical expressions such as if , therefore , and suppose .

sections.heading: Markup tokens.
sections.text: This category covers formula delimiters, structural punctuation within formulas, and LaTeX commands outside the mathematical and logical command lists. Examples include $ , \[ , and \] as delimiters, braces and subscript markers ( _ ) within formulas, and formatting commands such as \text and \left .

sections.heading: Whitespace tokens.
sections.text: This category contains tokens composed entirely of whitespace. Examples include a single space, consecutive spaces, a tab, or one or more line breaks. Leading spaces attached to a word do not make that token a whitespace token.

sections.heading: Other tokens.
sections.text: This category contains unassigned text and punctuation, special tokens, and tokens crossing incompatible category boundaries. Examples include ordinary prose words such as the and and , commas or periods in prose, and special tokens such as <|im_end|> .

sections.heading: Token boundaries.
sections.text: We label character spans and map them to the original tokens through UTF-8 byte spans, without retokenization. Ignoring whitespace, tokens spanning compatible mathematical or stylistic subtypes keep that category; incompatible mixtures are assigned to Other. Logical expressions are matched separately and merged into the mathematical group after this boundary handling.

sections.heading: C.3 Category-Level Aggregation
sections.text: The five displayed categories are disjoint and account for all response tokens in the 8,192 responses. For each category, we compute the mean absolute log-ratio within each response, average the eight response means within each question with equal weight, and then average over the 1,024 questions with equal weight. Every displayed group occurs in every response, so all eight responses contribute to every question’s category mean. For the mathematical group, we combine mathematical-content and logical-expression tokens within each response before computing its mean. This procedure gives responses equal weight regardless of length. The student–base and same-sign-filtered panels use exactly the same category positions and averaging order. For filtering, we multiply each student–base difference by 𝟏 [ r t d t > 0 ] \mathbf{1}[r_{t}d_{t}>0] ; opposite signs and exact zeros yield zero. Zeroed positions remain in the original category denominator, so the filtered means measure retained amplitude per original token.

sections.heading: C.4 Expression-Level Preference Statistics
sections.text: We consider alphabetic English strings with at least 50 occurrences across at least 20 questions, merging decoded tokens after lowercasing and stripping leading and trailing whitespace; subword fragments therefore remain separate strings. The word clouds in Figure 3 (a–b) show 50 representative strings for each sign: ten high-amplitude examples and forty lower-amplitude context strings. Within each panel, a monotone piecewise-linear size scale expands variation among the context strings while preserving larger sizes for the high-amplitude examples; all strings are horizontal, and color darkens with size. Figure 3 (c) uses six representative strings chosen by lexical function and observed sign: suppose , try , strategy , and idea express hypothesis formation, exploration, and planning, while straightforward and simplicity describe procedural ease. They occur in 280, 554, 112, 166, 47, and 110 questions, respectively, and we keep all their occurrences across the eight responses per question. For each string, we average its occurrences within each response, then the responses containing it within each question, and finally the questions containing it. We apply this same aggregation to d t d_{t} , its positive and negative parts, and those parts multiplied by 𝟏 [ r t d t > 0 ] \mathbf{1}[r_{t}d_{t}>0] . Rejected positions contribute zero and remain in the original denominators. The retained amplitude percentage divides the aggregated retained absolute amplitude by the aggregated original absolute amplitude.

sections.heading: Controlled settings.
sections.text: The original setting uses Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as teacher, Qwen3-1.7B as student, Qwen3-1.7B-Base as base, and DAPO-Math-17K. The GSM8K data setting retains the original models and samples 1,024 questions without replacement from the GSM8K training split ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , using the same surrounding prompt instructions. Each setting includes all eight responses to 1,024 questions, without correctness or length filtering. Sampling, scoring, and category definitions follow Appendix C . We compare uncentered log-probability differences on the initial student’s responses, and teacher-agreement filtering follows Section 3.2 , with rejected positions contributing zero to the original averages.

sections.heading: Larger OPD amplitudes at style-related positions.
sections.text: Table D1 shows that style-related positions receive larger mean absolute teacher–student log-ratios in both additional settings, with style-to-mathematics amplitude ratios of 3.262 for the 30B-A3B teacher and 5.646 on GSM8K. Changing the teacher alters the source of feedback on fixed responses, whereas changing the dataset also changes the trajectories being scored. Both comparisons reproduce the disparity identified in Section 3.1 : teacher–student disagreement assigns larger per-token coefficients to differences in expression.

sections.heading: Teacher agreement reduces the relative style amplitude.
sections.text: Across the two additional settings, gating removes 63.3–81.0% of the student–base style amplitude, compared with 57.1–57.2% of the mathematical amplitude. The style-to-mathematics ratio consequently falls in each setting, with the largest reduction on GSM8K, from 5.246 to 2.318. Because filtered positions remain in the original denominators, these reductions measure how much of each category’s acquired amplitude survives the teacher’s direction test. Both settings reproduce the observation in Section 3.2 : teacher selection changes the relative allocation of student-derived feedback, retaining proportionally less amplitude at style-related positions.

sections.heading: The magnitude source changes the gated balance.
sections.text: With the 30B-A3B teacher, gated student–base weighting gives a style-to-mathematics ratio of 3.520, compared with 3.739 for gated OPD. On GSM8K, the corresponding ratios are 2.318 and 3.811. Each comparison holds the sign mask fixed, so these differences come from the source of update magnitudes. Both comparisons reproduce the lower ratio from student-derived magnitudes observed for Qwen3-1.7B in Section 3.2 .

We first observe an amplitude disparity in this feedback: on math reasoning responses, style-related positions exhibit 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher–student log-probability difference of mathematical positions. Scaling OPD updates by these discrepancies thus directs much of the update strength toward matching the teacher’s expression. We instead take the student’s own pretrained base as a reference: the student–base difference records the token preferences acquired during post-training and provides supervision that does not depend on the student’s distance from the teacher. Building on this reference, we propose Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation ( SD-OPD ), which uses centered student–base differences as update coefficients, keeps each coefficient only when its sign agrees with centered teacher–student feedback, and recomputes the student signal every training round. Across 5 teacher–student configurations with Qwen3 students of 1.7B to 8B parameters, SD-OPD improves six-task mathematics average pass@1 (avg@16) over OPD by 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points. Teacher T T and base S B S_{B} remain frozen. 1 Introduction On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach in which a language model learns from a teacher on responses generated by its own current policy ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2023 ) . The teacher scores every token at prefixes the student visits, so supervision is dense and lies on the student’s own trajectories. As the student changes, new responses are sampled and scored, and the training distribution follows the student’s current behavior, as in imitation learning on learner-induced states ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . This combination of on-policy sampling and token-level feedback has supported both capability transfer from larger teachers to smaller students ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) and the consolidation of specialized teachers into a single model ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) . However, the effectiveness of OPD depends on how teacher feedback is constructed and weighted ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In sampled-token OPD, the magnitude of teacher–student log-probability differences determines the strength of token-level supervision ( Gu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Post-training also shifts a model’s preferences for wording and formatting ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) , so teacher–student disagreement reflects differences in expression as well as gaps in reasoning. Weighting updates by this disagreement thus spends update strength on the teacher’s expression as well as its reasoning. This raises two questions: how is update strength distributed across tokens, and can it come from a source other than teacher disagreement? For the first question, on DAPO-Math responses, style-related positions have 3.5 times the mean absolute teacher–student log-probability difference of mathematical positions (Figure 2 ). For the second, we compare the student with its own pretrained base ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , which records the token preferences the student has already acquired, independently of its distance from the teacher. These preferences include reasoning expressions such as suppose , try , and strategy , but their amplitude is also concentrated at style-related positions, with a style-to-mathematics ratio of 4.1, so they need selection. We select them by teacher sign agreement, keeping a student preference only where the teacher favors the same direction. This test retains very different shares of preferences with similar strength (Figure 3 ) and lowers the style-to-mathematics ratio to 3.1, whereas the same test with teacher–student magnitudes still leaves 3.7 (Section 3.2 ). These findings lead to Student-Delta On-Policy Distillation ( SD-OPD ; Figure 1 ). Centered student–base log-probability differences supply the coefficients, and a coefficient is kept only when its sign agrees with centered teacher–student feedback. The teacher thus decides which student preferences to develop, but its disagreement magnitude does not scale the updates. The teacher and base stay frozen, while the student signal is recomputed after each training round, so it covers both the initial post-training changes and those acquired during distillation. We evaluate SD-OPD in 5 teacher–student configurations with three teachers and Qwen3 students of 1.7B, 4B, and 8B parameters, using six mathematics benchmarks and matched rollout and response budgets. SD-OPD outperforms OPD on every benchmark in every configuration and achieves the highest six-task student average in all 5 configurations (Table 1 ). Average gains range from 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points over OPD and from 3.45 to 14.89 over ExOPD. Our contributions are as follows: • A diagnosis of how OPD weights its updates. We show that teacher–student disagreement is not a neutral measure of what the student should learn: its mean absolute magnitude is 3.5 times larger at style-related than at mathematical positions, the gap persists with a larger teacher and on GSM8K, and sign-agreement filtering does not remove it while teacher–student differences set the magnitude. • The student’s own post-training changes as a source of supervision. We show that the difference between a post-trained student and its pretrained base can set update strength, with the teacher deciding only which directions to reinforce. SD-OPD implements this division of roles and recomputes the student signal every round, so update strength follows what the current student prefers rather than how far it is from the teacher. It improves over OPD in every evaluated configuration and lets an 8B student exceed the average accuracy of its Qwen3-30B-A3B teacher. All panels share the scale, categories, and averaging procedure in Equation 2 ; filtered-out positions contribute zero and remain in the denominator. 2 Related Work On-policy knowledge distillation. Knowledge distillation transfers teacher predictions to a student ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , while sequence-level distillation trains on teacher-generated targets ( Kim and Rush, 2016 ) . Teacher-generated reasoning data extend this approach to mathematical and code reasoning ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Guha et al., 2026 ) . GKD and MiniLLM obtain supervision on student-generated sequences through distribution matching and reverse-KL policy optimization ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2023 ) . DistiLLM combines skew-divergence objectives with reuse of student outputs, while DistiLLM-2 contrasts teacher- and student-generated responses ( Ko et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) . Black-box OPD learns feedback from a discriminator trained on teacher and student text ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . Recent work also studies local distribution matching and token-specific supervision weights ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . In these methods, teacher outputs determine the strength of supervision; SD-OPD instead takes update strength from the student’s own post-training changes and uses the teacher only to select their direction. Self-distillation and contextual supervision. Context-conditioned self-teaching obtains additional information from reference solutions in Self-Distilled Reasoner ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , textual feedback in SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) , and demonstrations in SDFT ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . On-Policy Context Distillation also learns from a context-conditioned teacher, including configurations with different teacher and student sizes ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . In these approaches, the additional supervision comes from privileged information placed in the teacher’s context; in SD-OPD , it comes from the student’s own post-training history, measured against a fixed base model, with an independent teacher constraining its direction. Post-training differences and delta distillation. URIAL analyzes changes between aligned and base token distributions, including changes in expression ( Lin et al., 2024 ) ; we turn this comparison into a training signal. Policy–reference log-ratios connect preference optimization to implicit rewards ( Rafailov et al., 2023 ) ; implicit process reward models and PRIME extend this connection to dense reasoning feedback learned from outcome labels ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . G-OPD introduces a reference policy and reward scaling; its ExOPD variant studies extrapolation with both an initial-student reference and a teacher pre-RL reference ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . OPD 2 also uses centering and a same-sign condition, but its primary signal is a teacher–base difference ( Heo et al., 2026 ) . SD-OPD instead uses the current student’s changes relative to the student’s own base, recomputed every round, and lets teacher feedback decide which directions to reinforce. Appendix C gives generation and scoring details, and Appendix D repeats the category-level analyses with another teacher and on GSM8K. 3.1 Teacher–Student Disagreement Varies across Token Categories To compare teacher–student disagreement across token categories, we use the sampled-token log-ratio feedback studied in OPD ( Gu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . For response token y t y_{t} at prefix h t = ( x , y < t ) h_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) , this feedback is r t = log ⁡ p T ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) − log ⁡ p S 0 ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) . r_{t}=\log p_{T}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})-\log p_{S_{0}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t}). (1) We categorize token positions using fixed textual rules. Style-related positions include discourse wording, answer labels, and Markdown formatting, while mathematical positions include numbers, operators, formula variables, a fixed mathematical lexicon, and logical expressions. Markup, whitespace, and other tokens form separate groups; Appendix C details the classification. Because the categories differ in frequency (about 0.6 million style-related and 4.7 million mathematical tokens, both present in every response), we compare per-token means rather than totals. For positions 𝒯 i , j , c \mathcal{T}_{i,j,c} in category c c of response j j to question i i , we compute the per-token mean M i , j , c ​ ( r ) = 1 | 𝒯 i , j , c | ​ ∑ t ∈ 𝒯 i , j , c | r i , j , t | . M_{i,j,c}(r)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i,j,c}|}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_{i,j,c}}|r_{i,j,t}|. (2) We average these values equally over the eight responses to each question and then equally over questions, preventing longer responses from receiving extra weight. Style-related positions have larger feedback amplitudes. Figure 2 (a) shows mean absolute feedback of 1.226 at style-related positions and 0.347 at mathematical positions, a 3.5-fold difference. OPD uses this log-ratio as a coefficient in token-level policy gradients ( Gu et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , so for the initial student, style-related positions receive larger coefficients on average. For example, differences in wording or formatting receive large coefficients even when the student expresses the same mathematical idea. 3.2 Student Preferences and Teacher Selection Since teacher disagreement mixes expression with reasoning, we look for a reference that measures update strength from what the student has already learned. The student’s own pretrained base provides one: comparing student and base predictions at shared prefixes reveals preferences acquired during post-training, including how the student expresses mathematical reasoning ( Lin et al., 2024 ) . On the same responses and prefixes, we define d t = log ⁡ p S 0 ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) − log ⁡ p S B ​ ( y t ∣ h t ) . d_{t}=\log p_{S_{0}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t})-\log p_{S_{B}}(y_{t}\mid h_{t}). (3) The sign of d t d_{t} indicates whether the observed token has become more probable ( d t > 0 d_{t}>0 ) or less probable ( d t < 0 d_{t}<0 ) relative to the base at that prefix. Since the reference is the pretrained base, this difference summarizes cumulative changes across post-training. Acquired preferences favor exploration and planning. Figure 3 (a–b) shows the strings whose probability post-training raised or lowered most. The raised strings are reasoning moves rather than formatting: they form hypotheses and explore alternatives ( suppose , maybe , try ), plan and organize a solution ( strategy , idea , structure ), and test candidates ( plug , examine ). The lowered strings instead narrate routine computation ( calculations , distribute , rewrite ) or assert that a step is easy or correct ( straightforward , ensuring ), and their shifts are much smaller. Post-training has thus mainly added ways of deciding how to approach a problem, rather than removing old habits of describing computations. Beyond step 50, the separation persists, with further gradual entropy reduction in SD-OPD and continuing length fluctuations (Appendix B.1 ). 6 Conclusion We showed that a student’s existing post-training changes can drive continued on-policy distillation. Since teacher–student disagreement is several times larger at style-related than at mathematical positions, SD-OPD instead takes update strength from student–base differences, constrains their direction with teacher feedback, and refreshes the student source throughout training. Across 5 teacher–student configurations, SD-OPD improves all six mathematics benchmarks over OPD and achieves higher six-task averages than both OPD and ExOPD. Average gains over OPD range from 7.76 to 10.37 percentage points when either the teacher or the student size changes. The ablations show that both components are needed: reinforcing student preferences without teacher feedback collapses all six benchmarks to zero, and fixing the student source falls below OPD. Further work can examine which of the student’s own post-training changes provide useful supervision, how their value evolves during training, and how they can support continued learning across tasks. C.2 Token Categories We assign the five categories in Figure 2 using fixed English and Chinese phrase lists and textual rules, independently of model scores. Style-related tokens. This category covers discourse wording, answer labels, and Markdown formatting used to organize or present a response. Examples include let’s , next , and finally ; line-initial Answer or Solution labels; and Markdown markers such as # and ** . Mathematical tokens. This category covers numbers, operators, formula variables, mathematical vocabulary, and logical expressions used in derivations. Examples include numerals such as 3 3 and 12 12 , operators such as + + and = = , formula variables such as x x , and commands such as \frac and \sqrt . It also includes terms such as integer and triangle , and logical expressions such as if , therefore , and suppose . Markup tokens. This category covers formula delimiters, structural punctuation within formulas, and LaTeX commands outside the mathematical and logical command lists. Examples include $ , \[ , and \] as delimiters, braces and subscript markers ( _ ) within formulas, and formatting commands such as \text and \left . Whitespace tokens. This category contains tokens composed entirely of whitespace. Examples include a single space, consecutive spaces, a tab, or one or more line breaks. Leading spaces attached to a word do not make that token a whitespace token. Other tokens. This category contains unassigned text and punctuation, special tokens, and tokens crossing incompatible category boundaries. Examples include ordinary prose words such as the and and , commas or periods in prose, and special tokens such as <|im_end|> . Token boundaries. We label character spans and map them to the original tokens through UTF-8 byte spans, without retokenization. Ignoring whitespace, tokens spanning compatible mathematical or stylistic subtypes keep that category; incompatible mixtures are assigned to Other. Logical expressions are matched separately and merged into the mathematical group after this boundary handling.
